store.intro: Content-addressed, append-only. Objects are stored by SHA-256 hash; editing produces a new hash while the old one stays readable. The head is a mutable pointer; its moves are an append-only history.

tutorial.heading: Understanding the content store
tutorial.lead: The concepts behind this screen, before the jargon. The store keeps bytes and never destroys anything.

t1.title: Content-addressing
t1.body: An object is named not by a label or a number, but by its content itself. The same byte sequence always yields the same address; two different contents have two different addresses.

t2.title: The SHA-256 fingerprint
t2.body: That address is the SHA-256 fingerprint of the content — a hexadecimal digest computed over the bytes. It is both the storage key and the integrity proof: if the content changes, the fingerprint changes.

t3.title: An object is immutable
t3.body: Once stored under its fingerprint, an object never moves again. Its content stays readable as-is, indefinitely. You don't overwrite an object: you store a new one.

t4.title: The head, a mutable pointer
t4.body: The head is a mutable label binding a readable key (e.g. "doc") to a fingerprint. It is the only moving part: you point it at another fingerprint to "advance" the current version.

t5.title: Append-only history, idempotent Put
t5.body: Every head move is appended to an append-only history: nothing is erased, you only stack. Put is idempotent — identical content returns the same fingerprint, with no new row. Editing makes a NEW fingerprint; the old one stays readable. Nothing is ever destroyed.

example.heading: Try this
example.lead: A worked example that leans on the "Store" and "Move a head" controls below. Reproduce it step by step.

e1.title: 1) Store a first content
e1.body: In "Store content", enter hello and submit. You get its SHA-256 fingerprint: that is the address of the first object.

e2.title: 2) Point the "doc" head at it
e2.body: In "Move a head", set the key doc, click "Use last stored" to reuse the fingerprint, then move the head. The doc head now names hello.

e3.title: 3) Edit: store "hello v2"
e3.body: Store hello v2 (a new fingerprint), then move the doc head onto it. The head moves, the history now lists both moves, and the fingerprint of hello stays readable.

example.takeaway: Takeaway: editing overwrites nothing. A new fingerprint appears, the head advances, the history grows append-only — and every past version stays reachable by its fingerprint.

tutorial.heading: Understanding the execution contract
tutorial.lead: The concepts behind this screen, before the jargon. The contract is the root law every later step must obey — one file, two readers.

t1.title: One file, two readers
t1.body: The contract lives in docs/implementation_contract.md: a machine-readable YAML block (the harness reads it) topped by human-readable prose. Both say the same thing; the YAML is the canonical source, the prose is its projection.

t2.title: The per-step loop — nine phases
t2.body: Every AIDOS step follows the same ordered loop: grill-with-docs → BDD mirror → tdd → sensors → completeness → diagnose → UI+Playwright → improve-architecture → artifacts. You never skip a phase.

t3.title: Gate: computational or human
t3.body: Each phase carries a gate: computational if the harness can decide it alone, human if it needs a human judgement. That is what separates what self-certifies from what needs a decision.

t4.title: The granularity rule — five properties
t4.body: Every step is minimal (one capability), autonomous (testable alone), visualizable (a route + an e2e), non-destructive (never silently breaks) and chainable (leaves a stable phase).

t5.title: "Done is computed, never declared"
t5.body: You never declare a step done: it is computed — red set green ∧ prior green intact ∧ no monster. Any change to the contract goes through a ChangeSet and a semver bump; the screen only projects, it never writes.

example.heading: What a phase looks like
example.lead: A concrete example: the shape of one phase entry of the machine block — its id, label and gate. No input required; you read the contract as it is encoded.
example.body:
- id: tdd
  label: "/tdd to code"
  description: >
    red → green → refactor, in the step's own package.
  gate: computational
example.takeaway: Takeaway: every phase carries the same envelope — id, label, gate — and the table below is nothing more than the projection of these entries. To evolve the contract you don't edit it here: you go through a ChangeSet (coming S20) and bump the semver.

projects.title: Projects
projects.intro: The project is the first-rank Kernel concept that scopes every truth. Two users (or two apps) never collide in the singleton truth-store: every truth belongs to a project. A project is content-addressed (its SHA-256 digest), carries an active|archived|deleted lifecycle, and gets an isolated DAG root node. Written below the wall, append-only — deletion is soft (the hard GDPR delete is S116).

tutorial.heading: Understanding the KRDCore records
tutorial.lead: The concepts behind this screen, before the jargon. A record is a frozen truth, addressed by its content, never erased.

t1.title: Seven record families
t1.body: AIDOS's truth is filed into seven families: the idea (ideas.idea), then in the kernel the truth, the layer and the link (kernel.truth/layer/link), the mirror (mirrors.mirror), the ChangeSet (changesets.changeset) and the DAG phase (dag.phase). Each has its own table, but all share the same record shape.

t2.title: Content-addressed truth
t2.body: A record has no name: its id is the SHA-256 fingerprint of its canonical JSONB body. The same body always yields the same id; two different bodies have two different ids. The address is the content.

t3.title: Append-only: never overwrite
t3.body: A body is never modified. To "change" a truth, you INSERT a new record and mark the old one superseded_by its successor. Nothing is destroyed: the head moves, the history stacks.

t4.title: Version = fingerprint = licence to change
t4.body: The version is also a fingerprint of the content. It does not increment like a counter: it is recomputed. Knowing the current version is holding the licence to propose the next one — on the right base, with no collision.

t5.title: The wall: the screen never touches truth
t5.body: These tables are ABOVE the line: the agent role has READ (SELECT) only. Every truth-write goes through propose → ChangeSet → human approval (coming S20). This screen reads the records; it never writes any.

body.statement: A record id is the SHA-256 fingerprint of its canonical body.

example.takeaway: Takeaway: every record carries the same envelope — id, version, superseded_by, created_at — plus a JSONB body specific to its family. To create a real one, you don't write it here: you go through propose → ChangeSet (coming S20).

wall.title: The wall
wall.intro: The wall is the single permission boundary: the agent writes projections (below the waterline), never kernel / mirrors / fitness (above). This screen visualizes the line, the guarded zones, and a feed of block events. It writes no truth (read-only) — the wall is held by the Go hook (level 1) and the Postgres GRANTs (level 2), not by this screen.

tutorial.heading: Understanding the wall
tutorial.lead: The concepts behind this screen, before the jargon. The wall does not decide what is true; it only forbids the agent from writing it in passing.

t1.title: A waterline
t1.body: Above = truth (kernel, mirrors, fitness), frozen. Below = projections (emitted code, adapters), free. The agent writes below, never above.

t2.title: Defense in depth, two levels
t2.body: Level 1: the PreToolUse hook (Go) refuses the write before it happens. Level 2: the Postgres GRANTs — the aidos_agent role has no write privilege on those schemas. Even if level 1 is bypassed, level 2 holds.

t3.title: An actionable refusal, never a prison
t3.body: Every refusal comes back as a BlockReason: a code (AGENT_WRITE_ABOVE_WATERLINE), a severity, an explanation, and a how_to_fix that names the door.

t4.title: The only door to the kernel
t4.body: idea → mirror → /goal → approval. The approved ChangeSet is applied by the aidos role; truth is never written directly.

example.heading: A wall refusal in action
example.lead: The agent tries to write back/kernel/records/store.go (above the line). The hook refuses and returns this BlockReason — writing nothing.
example.takeaway: Move the target below the line (e.g. back/gen/order.go) and the verdict becomes allow — the wall only fences truth.

mirrors.title: The ratchet
mirrors.intro: The ratchet replays every materialized mirror and compares each verdict to the recorded green baseline. The moment a baseline-green mirror turns red on the candidate, the merge is rejected — RED_REGRESSION — before the merge, never after. This screen replays the ratchet over a declared candidate scenario and shows the merge verdict. The ratchet reads the mirror set and writes only its own run-log (runtime.mirror_runs, below the waterline) — no truth is written from the screen.

tutorial.heading: Understanding the ratchet
tutorial.lead: The ratchet (KRD iteration 3) is the mechanism that prevents a silent regression. It replays every mirror and compares to the recorded green.

t1.title: Replay every mirror
t1.body: On every merge candidate, replay each living, materialized mirror — not just the ones you think are touched.

t2.title: Green at baseline is a promise
t2.body: A mirror green at the baseline is a promise not to break it. The ratchet only protects what was green; an already-red mirror does not regress.

t3.title: A regression rejects the merge
t3.body: A mirror green at baseline and red on the candidate is a regression. The ci-ratchet hook returns a RED_REGRESSION BlockReason and a non-zero exit — the merge is rejected.

t4.title: Append-only run-log
t4.body: Every replay writes one immutable row to runtime.mirror_runs (content-addressed). A re-run appends a row, never updates one — the ratchet's history cannot be rewritten.

verdict.allowed: ALLOWED — no baseline-green mirror regressed. The merge is allowed.
verdict.rejected: REJECTED — {code}: a baseline-green mirror is red on the candidate. The merge is rejected.

block.heading: Regression detected
block.explanation: The ratchet refuses the merge: one or more baseline-green mirrors are red on the candidate. Repair the behaviour until it is green again, or open a /goal if the change is intentional.

mirrors.footer: Enforced capability: back/mcp/mirror-runner (replay + run-log) + back/hooks/ci-ratchet (merge gate) — projected here by lib/mirrors.ts.

mirrorHealth.title: Mirror health
mirrorHealth.intro: The bicephalous body made checkable: a truth (a kernel layer) has two heads — the intention in the Kernel, the proof in the Mirror. The completeness law demands that no truth is left without a living mirror (no_truth_without_mirror) and no mirror reflects nothing (no_orphan_mirror). A truth without a mirror, or an orphan mirror, is a MONSTER — and a monster is red. This panel computes the law over a declared cut of mirrors ⋈ kernel, read-only: it reads truth, it writes nothing.

tutorial.heading: Understanding the completeness law
tutorial.lead: A Mirror is the executable proof of a truth, typed by five fields. Completeness checks that the intention-head / proof-head symmetry holds everywhere.

t1.title: Five fields type the mirror
t1.body: reflects (the layer it proves @version), test_kind, cert_language, authority (above | below), liveness (alive | dead). Declaring a mirror means filling these in (KRD §34).

t2.title: no_truth_without_mirror
t2.body: Every kernel layer must have at least one living mirror of each test_kind its kind requires (recorded profile, KRD §90). Otherwise: a hole, a monster, red.

t3.title: no_orphan_mirror
t3.body: Every mirror must reflect a real layer @version. A mirror whose target is gone (a superseded version) is an orphan: its liveness is dead, it is a monster, red.

t4.title: Executable, or it does not count
t4.body: A mirror whose cert_language is not executable as a deterministic sensor (prose, an LLM-judge alone) does NOT count toward completeness (KRD §805). The layer stays a monster.

sensors.title: Sensors
sensors.intro: After each agent diff below the waterline, the PostToolUse hook resolves the changed code and runs the computational sensor suite (gofmt, vet, lint, archtest, affected). On any red sensor: on_fail → block, with an actionable BlockReason (code SENSOR_FAILED). This screen projects runtime.sensor_runs (read-only) — the sensors are enforced by the harness-invoked Go hook, never from this screen.

completeness.title: Completeness / monster
completeness.intro: At Stop, the Go hook reads the current cut of mirrors ⋈ kernel, computes the monster set (S06) and applies the gate (S12): block on any monster (BlockReason, code MONSTER), pass on a complete cut. A monster is a truth with no living mirror (no_truth_without_mirror) or an orphan mirror (no_orphan_mirror, liveness=dead). This panel projects runtime.completeness_runs (read-only) — the gate is enforced by the harness-invoked Go hook, never from this screen.
completeness.emptyMonsterSet: No monster — the cut is complete, Stop may proceed.
completeness.completeBody: When every layer has at least one living, executable, correctly-reflecting mirror, the monster set is empty and the verdict is COMPLETE.

expr.title: Expr DSL
expr.subtitle: The typed JSON AST that makes a button's conditions — visible_when, enabled_when — executable and versionable as kernel artifacts, never free code.
expr.intro: Behaviour is a constrained artifact (KRD §24.5): a button's condition is not free code but a typed tree — lit / ref / call / obj / arr — over a CLOSED function catalogue and $-rooted refs. Stored content-addressed in kernel.expr, evaluated by a pure, deterministic function. This panel projects those ASTs (SELECT-only role): the typed tree, its roots, and the evaluated visible_when result.

tutorialSteps.kinds: Five node kinds, and only five: lit (literal value), ref ($-rooted path into the Env), call (a closed-catalogue function applied to argument exprs), obj / arr (structural composers).
tutorialSteps.catalogue: The catalogue is a CLOSED allow-list: no escape to arbitrary code. now / uuid / randomToken resolve through injected providers, so evaluation stays deterministic (same AST + same Env ⇒ same value).
tutorialSteps.roots: A root is an entry point into the Env: $.input, $.auth.user, $.cart… The .length segment yields the length of an array or string.
tutorialSteps.example: Canonical example: $.cart.items.length > 0 — the checkout button's visible_when. True when the cart has items, false when it is empty.

expr.rejectedExplain: A call to a function absent from the catalogue (e.g. "exec") is REJECTED at Parse — it is never evaluated. That is the "no free code" guarantee: the catalogue is closed.
expr.rejectedExample: call "exec" [ lit "rm -rf /" ]  →  rejected: unknown function "exec" (closed allow-list)
expr.footer: Source: back/kernel/expr (the AST + the pure evaluator, SELECT-only wall on kernel.expr) — projected here by lib/expr.ts, reproducibility mirror lib/expr.test.ts.

policy.title: Policy DSL
policy.subtitle: Authorization as an artifact: an ALLOW/DENY rule tree (∀), versioned and content-addressed, never free code.
policy.intro: A policy answers one question — “is this authorized?” — with a recursive tree: combinators all/any/not, comparisons eq/gt/lt, predicates exists/matches over a $-rooted selector. The combination law (§93): every ALLOW passes, any DENY blocks.
policy.tutorialLead: One example is enough: the canPlaceOrder policy of the createOrder operation (KRD §93).

tutorialSteps.scope: The scope says WHERE the policy applies: here OPERATION “createOrder”.
tutorialSteps.rule: The rule is an all([…]) tree: all three leaves must hold.
tutorialSteps.effect: The ALLOW effect is a gate: the policy authorizes IF the rule holds, else DENY.
tutorialSteps.example: Try a context below: a non-empty cart owned by an authed user yields ALLOW; otherwise DENY.

policy.tryLead: Each context is evaluated against canPlaceOrder. The decision is total: ALLOW or DENY.
policy.footer: A policy is a SOURCE truth above the waterline. It is written only via the aidos CLI through an approved ChangeSet — never from a screen. This page projects kernel.policy (SELECT-only role).

operation.title: Operation DSL
operation.subtitle: Workflow as an artifact: an operation body = an ordered list of typed steps, run state → command → events (N2), never free code.
operation.intro: An operation chains six verbs — validate, authorize, read, mutate, branch, return — read from its kernel AST. The interpreter walks them in order against a state ($.input, $.auth, named slots) and returns the ordered event list + the return ref. authorize delegates to the Policy DSL: a DENY short-circuits everything.
operation.tutorialLead: One example is enough: the createOrder operation (KRD §93), proven by the createOrder/happy fixture.

tutorialSteps.pipeline: The pipeline is an ordered sequence of steps: validate → authorize → read → mutate → mutate → return.
tutorialSteps.authorize: authorize delegates to the canPlaceOrder policy; a DENY short-circuits before any mutate (no event emitted).
tutorialSteps.events: Each mutate emits an event, in step order: OrderCreated then CartCleared.
tutorialSteps.fixture: The state → command → events fixture is the truth (N2): it PASSes when the trace matches exactly.

operation.traceLead: Given state → command → ordered events. The badge shows whether the fixture passes.
operation.footer: An operation is a SOURCE truth above the waterline; the interpreter is its projection (below the line). A mutate reaches the world only through an injected Mutator seam — never a direct write. This page projects kernel.operation and the fixture result.

control.title: Control & Action
control.subtitle: Behaviour in DSL all the way down to the button: a control-spec IS a button-source (visible-when / enabled-when), an action-spec BINDS it to an operation — never free code on the truth side.
control.intro: The « checkout-button » control declares visible_when / enabled_when (Expr DSL) and triggers → action. The « checkout-submit » action binds operation createOrder and declares its effects (on_success / on_error). The rendered button and its onClick are a later projection, guarded by these two fixtures.

control.tutorialLead: One example is enough: the checkout-button control (KRD §24.1) and the checkout-submit action (KRD §24.2), proven by their fixtures.

tutorialSteps.control: The control is a button-source: visible_when ($.cart.items.length > 0) and enabled_when ($.form.valid && !$.submitting) are Expr DSL ASTs, not code.

whyBlocked.title: Why blocked
whyBlocked.subtitle: Every refusal is actionable
whyBlocked.intro: A wall without a BlockReason becomes a prison (KRD §44.5). Every KRD refusal comes back explained: a code, a severity, an explanation, and a non-empty how_to_fix resolution path. This panel renders a BlockReason exactly as "aidos explain <CODE>" does — same fields, same order — for the three canonical codes (MISSING_MIRROR, MISSING_AUTHORITY, OUT_OF_SCOPE) plus the inherited wall code (AGENT_WRITE_ABOVE_WATERLINE). Read-only: the BlockReason is produced at refusal time by sites that already exist (the wall, completeness, the scope/authority checks); this panel projects it, it does not erect a wall.
whyBlocked.tutorialBody: Each card is a BlockReason. The badge at the top is the machine code of the refusal. The severity states the gravity (blocking: the action is halted). The explanation states why. The numbered how_to_fix list is the resolution path: follow the steps in order to lift the block. This is the same output as "aidos explain <CODE>" in the terminal.
whyBlocked.exampleBody: A change touches a truth with no living mirror. The refusal returns with code MISSING_MIRROR and the path: write the mirror, get authority approval, rerun aidos check. The wall always names the door out.
whyBlocked.footer: Source: back/runtime/blockreason (the canonical type) rendered by aidos explain — projected here by lib/why-blocked.ts. BlockReason is Runtime plumbing below the waterline, never a kernel truth.

truthTyping.title: Type the true before the ratchet bites
truthTyping.subtitle: TruthKind + VerifiabilityLevel
truthTyping.intro: Every truth declares its epistemic type (TruthKind) and its verification mode (VerifiabilityLevel) before it enters — or not — the kernel (KRD §13.4–13.5). The ratchet only bites what is certifiable: a truth with no TruthKind is rejected; a non-verifiable truth is routed to /spike (the ratchet stays OFF — NOT a failure). Read-only: this panel renders the pure classifier's verdict; it never writes truth (the wall). Truth-writes go via propose → ChangeSet → approval.
truthTyping.tutorialBody: Each row is a candidate truth. The TruthKind chip states the EPISTEMIC type of the claim (one of seven: behavioral, structural, experiential, economic, regulatory, statistical, exploratory) — it is not the mirror's test_kind. The VerifiabilityLevel chip states whether the ratchet can bite this signal (one of five: deterministic, statistical, delayed, human_judged, unverifiable). The routing badge is the verdict: green KERNEL (admitted), amber /SPIKE (routed out of the kernel), red REJECTED (no TruthKind, or unknown TruthKind — with the BlockReason code). Only deterministic opens the kernel door.
truthTyping.exampleBody: An experiential truth whose VerifiabilityLevel is unverifiable cannot be proven by an exact test. KRD does not certify it: it is routed to /spike to be made falsifiable, then /harvest later. Routed to /spike is not a failure — it is the method's honesty: "here I cannot prove."
truthTyping.footer: Source: back/kernel/truthtyping (the pure classifier) — projected here by lib/truth-typing.ts. The verdict is computed, never declared; the typing is the kernel's rule (KRD §13.4–13.5), this screen only enforces it read-only.

scopes.title: Scope — no truth is universal by default
scopes.subtitle: TruthScope (KRD §13.7)
scopes.intro: A TruthScope is one of the four qualifiers of a truth (KRD §13.6): it says WHERE / WHEN / FOR-WHOM a truth holds — region, tenant, target, time_window, user_segment, environment. The rule (§13.7): "A truth without a scope is suspect. A decision reused out of scope is a structural hallucination." So an active truth must carry a scope, unless it is explicitly global (region "*", a deliberate escape hatch — never the implicit default). Read-only: this screen renders the pure guard's verdict; it never writes truth (the wall). Every write / rescope goes via propose → ChangeSet → approval.
scopes.tutorialBody: Each row is a candidate truth. The status chip gives its lifecycle (KRD §44.2: active, deprecated, shadowed, removed) — the rule binds ACTIVE truths only. The scope chips give its non-empty dimensions (region, target, user_segment, environment, time_window, tenant), taken verbatim from §13.7. The verdict badge is computed by the pure guard: green ACCEPTED (a scoped active truth, or a non-active exempt one), blue GLOBAL (explicit) when region is "*", red REJECTED — active truth without a scope for an active truth with no scope at all. The authority badge marks the scope as an above-the-line Kernel qualifier.
scopes.exampleBody: An active truth with no scope is rejected: "active truth without a scope". The ONLY way to make it universal is to say so — region "*" — which yields the GLOBAL (explicit) badge. Global is never implicit: an empty scope is NOT global. This is the method's honesty: a truth reused out of its scope would be a structural hallucination.
scopes.footer: Source: back/kernel/scope (the pure guard) — projected here by lib/scope.ts. The verdict is computed, never declared; the rule "no truth is universal by default" is the kernel's (KRD §13.7), this screen only enforces it read-only.

authorities.title: The AuthorityGraph — replacing "the human" with an explicit authority
authorities.subtitle: AuthorityGraph (KRD §13.8)
authorities.intro: An AuthorityGraph is one of the four truth qualifiers (KRD §13.6): it says WHO approves, vetoes or escalates a truth's admission, keyed by { domain, truth_kind }. The rule (§13.8): "every above-the-line truth must have an explicit authority owner." A regulatory rule, a UX rule, a security policy and a product decision are not approved by the same authority. Read-only: this screen renders the pure decider's verdict; it never writes truth (the wall). Any write / reauthorize goes through propose → ChangeSet → approval.
authorities.tutorialBody: The graph card names the domain (checkout), the truth_kind (regulatory, one of the seven §13.4 epistemic kinds) and the three role lists: approvers (who must all approve), veto (who blocks regardless of approvers), escalation (whom a partial approval is escalated to). The admission table runs the pure decider over each candidate row: the decision badge is computed — green ADMITTED (all approvers present, no veto), red BLOCKED (no approver ⇒ MISSING_AUTHORITY_APPROVAL, or a veto present ⇒ VETOED), amber ESCALATED (partial approval, routed to escalation). A block always carries an actionable BlockReason (code + how_to_fix) — the wall is not a prison (KRD §44.5).
authorities.exampleHeading: Example — a regulatory truth without legal approval is blocked
authorities.exampleBody: A regulatory rule submitted with no approval is BLOCKED with code MISSING_AUTHORITY_APPROVAL; its how_to_fix names the door: assign_authority then obtain_legal_approval. That is the S16 done criterion. Conversely a security veto dominates: even approved by legal and product_owner, a vetoed rule stays BLOCKED / VETOED — a veto is never bypassed. A partial approval (product_owner only, legal missing) is ESCALATED to architecture_board.
authorities.footer: Source: back/kernel/authority (the pure decider) — projected here by lib/authority.ts. The decision is computed, never declared; the rule "every above-the-line truth must have an explicit authority owner" is the kernel's (KRD §13.8), this screen only enforces it read-only.

linkGraph.title: The six versioned links — everything points at a VERSION, never an identity
linkGraph.subtitle: Link (KRD §41)
linkGraph.intro: A link points at a VERSION (id@version), never a bare identity: that is the whole point of KRD §41. The six kinds are a CLOSED set: projects_to, derives_from, contracts_with, triggers, binds, mirrors. When the target's head moves, the consumer's pinned version no longer matches — the link is stale (red); when the target has no head at all, the link is absent (red), dangling loudly (KRD §42, the red wave). Read-only: this screen renders the status resolved by the pure decider; it never writes truth (the wall). Any write goes via propose → ChangeSet → approval.
linkGraph.tutorialBody: Each edge is a link of one of the six kinds, labelled with its kind and its pinned to target (id@version). The colour is computed by the pure resolver (lib/links.ts, the projection of back/kernel/links) against the current heads: GREEN = pinned exactly to head; RED = stale (pinned to a version that is no longer head) or absent (the target has no head). Toggle the heads with the button: under "head present" the binds edge checkout-submit → createOrder@v3 is green; under "target absent" the same edge turns RED / absent — a link to an absent version is red.
linkGraph.exampleHeading: Example — a link to an absent version is red
linkGraph.exampleBody: The binds edge checkout-submit → createOrder@v3 is GREEN while createOrder's head is v3. Remove createOrder from the version DAG (no head at all) and the link does not vanish silently: it is rendered RED / absent, inspectable, ready to seed the red wave (KRD §42). This is the S17 done criterion. A link pinned to a version that is no longer head (e.g. createOrder@v2) is rendered stale, red as well.
linkGraph.footer: Source: back/kernel/links (the pure resolver) — projected here by lib/links.ts. The status is computed, never declared; the rule "every link points at a version, and a link to an absent version is red" is the kernel's (KRD §41–§42), this screen only enforces it read-only.

truthTree.title: The truth tree — a composite is green only if its own mirror AND all its children are green
truthTree.subtitle: composes (KRD §108–§112)
truthTree.intro: The 7th link composes is the mereology link: a whole contains a part, version-pinned and weighted (load-bearing | cosmetic). The completeness law becomes recursive (KRD §109): aggregate_complete(L) := own_mirror(L)==GREEN ∧ ∀ child via composes : aggregate_complete(child). A red child reddens the aggregated parent — THE done criterion. The weights and the activation_threshold (KRD §112) are DECLARED above the line, never learned. Read-only: this screen renders the verdict computed by the pure function; it never writes truth (the wall). Any write goes through propose → ChangeSet → approval.
truthTree.tutorialBody: The tree follows the KRD §114 worked example: product → journey → view → control (plus a cosmetic helptext leaf). Each node shows its own_mirror verdict AND its recursive AGGREGATE verdict, computed by the pure aggregate (lib/truth-tree.ts, the projection of back/kernel/composes). Each edge shows its composes weight (load-bearing | cosmetic) and pinned version; each composite shows its declared activation_threshold. Toggle the scenario: all-green ⇒ the product is GREEN; the load-bearing control leaf RED ⇒ the fall-back-up reddens view, journey and product, and the drill-down from the product names the control; a cosmetic change below threshold leaves the product GREEN.
truthTree.exampleHeading: Example — a red load-bearing child reddens the aggregated parent
truthTree.exampleBody: Under all-green, the product aggregates GREEN (its own mirror green ∧ all children green). Flip the control leaf (load-bearing) RED: the view's aggregate reddens, then the journey's, then the product's — compositional truth climbs the load-bearing chain. The drill-down from the product names the offending control. That is S18's done criterion. Conversely, a change confined to the cosmetic helptext leaf keeps activation (0.0) below the threshold (1.0): the product stays GREEN — "pin a defect, not a change" (KRD §112).
truthTree.drillEmpty: All green: no red child to descend into.
truthTree.footer: Source: back/kernel/composes (the pure recursive aggregate) — projected here by lib/truth-tree.ts. The verdict is computed, never declared; the recursive law (a composite is green iff its own mirror and all its children are, KRD §109) and the declared weights/thresholds (KRD §112) are the kernel's — this screen only applies them read-only.

redPropagation.title: Weighted propagation
redPropagation.subtitle: KRD §112 · §114
redPropagation.intro: The red wave along composes is weighted and thresholded, not a blind cascade: each composes link carries a declared weight (cosmetic | load-bearing | critical), the parent carries a declared activation_threshold, and the aggregate only reddens when the cumulative activation of changed children reaches the threshold. A cosmetic change does not redden the parent; a critical weight without weight evidence is rejected at admission. Weights and thresholds are declared, never learned.
redPropagation.tutorialBody: The tree shows the « cart » view and its three controls, each link drawn by its weight thickness (cosmetic thin, load-bearing thick, critical thickest). The fire table applies fire_parent: activation ← Σ weight(changed children); if activation ≥ threshold the aggregate is RED, else GREEN. The admission table applies the §2463 discipline: a critical link is admitted only if it carries weight evidence (a recorded reference, e.g. an incident id).
redPropagation.exampleBody: The « cart » view composes checkout-button (load-bearing), promo-field (load-bearing) and help-link (cosmetic), declared threshold 1. A change to help-link gives activation 0 < 1 → the aggregate stays GREEN (the done criterion: a cosmetic change does not redden the parent). A change to checkout-button gives activation 1 ≥ 1 → the aggregate turns RED. Declaring promo-field critical with no evidence is rejected with CRITICAL_WEIGHT_WITHOUT_EVIDENCE; with the evidence INC-2026-014, it is accepted.
redPropagation.footer: Read-only projection of back/kernel/propagation — weights and thresholds are declared (never learned); every truth-write goes via propose → ChangeSet → approval (the wall).

redWave.title: Red wave
redWave.subtitle: Impact / RedWorkQueue
redWave.intro: After a kernel bump, the red wave IS EXACTLY the set of stale links (KRD §42) — computed, never hunted. It STARTS at the mirror, then cascades to the projections (api/db/types/operation/action/button), and drains into the RedWorkQueue. Pick a bump and fire the wave: an entity change reddens api/db/types; a button change reddens its view iff the button is load-bearing.
redWave.tutorialBody: Pick a bump from the list, then read the computed wave. Each item is a RedWorkItem: its target (a mirror or a projection), its reason (version_stale) and its status (open — scheduling, claim/lease, is a later step). The items are ordered mirror-first (the mirror first, §42/§98) and grouped by layer. The same pure function computes this wave in Go (redwave.Impact), in the CLI (aidos impact) and here — one source, no drift.
redWave.emptyWave: Empty wave — no stale link, nothing to reopen (a cosmetic change does not propagate, §112).
redWave.orderLabel: Order: from the mirror to the projections (mirror-first, §42/§98).
redWave.bumpEntity: Entity bump — Order v1 → v2 (reddens the mirror then api/db/types)
redWave.bumpLoadBearing: Load-bearing button bump — submit-btn v1 → v2 (reddens checkout-view)
redWave.bumpCosmetic: Cosmetic button bump — label-btn v1 → v2 (does NOT redden the view)
redWave.exampleBody: The Order entity bump reopens its mirror first (Order.schema.fixture), then its projections api/db/types — the wave starts at the mirror (the done criterion, part 1). The load-bearing submit-btn button bump reddens checkout-view (part 2). The cosmetic label-btn button bump does NOT redden checkout-view (the negative): the wave is empty.
redWave.footer: Read-only projection of back/runtime/redwave — the wave is computed (never hunted) and writes no truth; the real enqueue goes through the PostKernelChange hook below the waterline.

causedBy.title: caused_by link
causedBy.subtitle: Backward causality · FKE-35.1
causedBy.intro: The caused_by link is the SEVENTH versioned edge — the BACKWARD causal edge, the inverse of the red wave (impacts, S22). "A caused_by B" means B is a candidate cause of A's redness. Pick a graph and run the deterministic trace: from a red symptom, Trace enumerates its candidate causes (nearest first), the same graph + symptom always yielding the same chain; a cycle is REFUSED. It is the substrate the WhyTree (FK13) builds on.
causedBy.tutorialBody: Pick a causal graph then run the trace. The cause chain lists the candidate ids ordered nearest to farthest (hop distance ascending, then by id) — the same pure function computes this trace in Go (causedby.Trace) and here, one source, no drift. A root symptom (a leaf) has no upstream cause. A cyclic graph (A caused_by B caused_by A) is REFUSED with CAUSED_BY_CYCLE — a cause chain cannot loop. The first edge's kernel.link body is shown: changing the pinned cause version yields a NEW version (content-addressed, append-only, never a mutation).
causedBy.emptyChain: Root cause — no upstream cause (a leaf of the caused_by graph).
causedBy.cycleRefused: Cycle refused — a cause chain cannot loop
causedBy.caseChain: Checkout chain — checkout-accept ← createOrder ← Order / authzPolicy ← add_total_col
causedBy.caseLeaf: Root cause — add_total_col (a leaf, no cause)
causedBy.footer: Read-only projection of back/kernel/causedby — the trace is computed (never guessed) and writes no truth; freezing a caused_by edge goes idea → mirror → /goal → human approval (the aidos CLI role, never the agent).

whyTree.title: WhyTree — /why gesture
whyTree.subtitle: The 5-whys redressed · FKE-35.1
whyTree.intro: The /why gesture builds a WhyTree from a red symptom: it walks caused_by (FK12) upward to the candidate causes, admits ONLY REPRODUCED causes (anti-confabulation — a cause you cannot make fail is rejected), and terminates OBLIGATORILY in an anti-recurrence mirror (root → /learn → mirror → red wave). A WhyTree with no terminal mirror is REFUSED (WHYTREE_NO_MIRROR). Pick a scenario and run /why.
whyTree.tutorialBody: Pick a scenario then run /why. The tree lists the REPRODUCED candidate causes (nearest first), names the ROOT cause (the deepest), then shows the terminal anti-recurrence mirror /learn freezes on the root (root → /learn → mirror → targeted red wave). The same pure function computes this tree in Go (whytree.Build) and here — the judge is the reproduction bool, never a prompt. Three refusals: no terminal mirror → WHYTREE_NO_MIRROR; a non-reproduced cause → WHYTREE_CAUSE_NOT_REPRODUCED (anti-confabulation); a caused_by cycle → CAUSED_BY_CYCLE (no partial tree). The content-addressed kernel.link body is shown.
whyTree.leafNote: Root symptom — no reproduced upstream cause (it is its own root).
whyTree.redWaveNote: This mirror, frozen at /goal, bumps the root's hash and triggers a targeted red wave (the worklist).
whyTree.caseIncident: Incident → tree → root mirror (checkout-accept, root add_total_col)
whyTree.errNoMirror: WHYTREE_NO_MIRROR — a WhyTree must end in an anti-recurrence mirror
whyTree.errNotReproduced: WHYTREE_CAUSE_NOT_REPRODUCED — a non-reproducible cause is rejected (anti-confabulation)
whyTree.errCycle: CAUSED_BY_CYCLE — a cause chain cannot loop (no partial tree)
whyTree.errMismatch: WHYTREE_TERMINAL_MISMATCH — the terminal mirror does not reflect the root cause
whyTree.errProvenance: UNKNOWN_PROVENANCE — provenance outside the set (incident | mirror | human)
whyTree.footer: Read-only projection of back/kernel/whytree — the tree is computed (never guessed) and writes no truth; freezing the terminal anti-recurrence mirror goes idea → mirror → /learn → /goal → human approval (the aidos CLI role, never the agent).

lexicon.title: Lexicon Kernel — inter-layer linter
lexicon.subtitle: Ubiquitous language · FKE-21
lexicon.intro: A concept must be RECOGNISABLE in every layer: human, BDD, code, test, DB, API, event, log, metric, MCP, skill, agent, doc, CI, policy, memory (the 16 layers, FKE-21). The Lexicon Kernel binds ONE concept to its legal symbol in each layer — a single source. The PURE linter detects a symbol out of lexicon, per layer: a language drift made verifiable by computation. Rename a table out of lexicon → red (RENAMED). Pick a scenario and run the linter.
lexicon.tutorialBody: Pick a scenario then run the linter. For each observed symbol the linter checks: is the layer one of the 16 (else UNKNOWN_LAYER); does the lexicon pin a symbol for this concept in this layer (else UNKNOWN_SYMBOL); does the observed symbol equal the lexicon's (else RENAMED — the symbol drifted). The same pure function computes these drifts in Go (lexicon.Lint) and here — the judge is a set-membership check, never a prompt. No drift = green. The content-addressed kernel.link body of the lexicon (the storage fork tranché here: a lexicon rides inside a kernel.link, link_kind:lexicon) is shown.
lexicon.cleanNote: Clean — every observed symbol is IN lexicon (no drift).
lexicon.caseRenamedTable: Renamed table out of lexicon (return_requests → orders_returns) — RED (RENAMED)
lexicon.caseUnknownSymbol: Layer not named in the lexicon (log) — UNKNOWN_SYMBOL
lexicon.driftRenamed: RENAMED — symbol out of lexicon (the concept is named otherwise here)
lexicon.driftUnknownSymbol: UNKNOWN_SYMBOL — the lexicon pins no symbol for this concept in this layer
lexicon.driftUnknownLayer: UNKNOWN_LAYER — layer outside the 16 closed layers (FKE-21)
lexicon.footer: Read-only projection of back/kernel/lexicon — the drifts are computed (never guessed) and write no truth; freezing/updating a lexicon goes idea → mirror → /goal → human approval (the aidos CLI role, never the agent).

toolProjection.title: Tooling projections
toolProjection.subtitle: Emitted tooling files · FKE-20
toolProjection.intro: CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / .cursorrules / memory-bank are NOT truth — they are DERIVED VIEWS, emitted from the kernels (policy / memory / style / architecture / agent-profile), the same way Go structs or TS types are projected from the entity AST. Because they are derived, they are HASH-PROTECTED: each file carries the source-hash of the kernels it is the projection of. A hand-edit changes the bytes without changing the source-hash — it is detected. Same kernels → byte-identical files. Pick a target and emit.
toolProjection.tutorialBody: Pick a target (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / .cursorrules / memory-bank.md) then EMIT: the rendered file (with the protection footer carrying the source-hash) appears. Each target carries only the kernel kinds it is the view of (CLAUDE.md = policies + architecture + style; AGENTS.md = agent-profile; memory-bank = memory; .cursorrules = policies + style) — no double-typing, no new truth. Check the clean file (no drift, green) or a HAND-EDITED file (the source-hash matches the marker but the bytes differ → HAND_EDITED, red). The same pure function computes the emission in Go (toolproject.Emit) and here — the judge is a deterministic render + a byte comparison, never a prompt.
toolProjection.noDrift: Clean — the file is the exact projection of the kernels (no drift).
toolProjection.driftHandEdited: HAND_EDITED — the body was hand-edited under a valid marker
toolProjection.driftMissingMarker: MISSING_MARKER — the file carries no AIDOS source-hash marker
toolProjection.driftStaleHash: STALE_HASH — the kernels changed, the file was not re-emitted
toolProjection.footer: Read-only projection of back/kernel/toolproject — the files are emitted (never hand-edited) and write no truth; freezing/updating a ToolingKernel goes idea → mirror → /goal → human approval (the aidos CLI role, never the agent).

techSpec.title: Technical spec & technical tests
techSpec.subtitle: Two assembled projections
techSpec.intro: The functional ↔ technical split adds no skeleton row: a 'technical specification' is a VIEW that assembles declarations that already exist. AIDOS renders it 'every time' as TWO deterministic projections per kernel: the Technical Specification Sheet (Contract F5 + Model F4 + the OSI stack if networked + facet specs S/B/R/V/M + linked ADRs) and the Technical Test Suite (N4/N5 + per-OSI-layer tests + facet tests). Zero new truth: every assembled element traces to an input declaration. Same kernels → byte-identical files. Pick a kernel and a projection, then assemble.
techSpec.tutorialBody: Pick a kernel (networked CheckoutAPI / pure-function Scorer) and a projection (Sheet / Suite) then ASSEMBLE: the rendered file (with the protection footer carrying the source-hash) appears, ranged by axis (OSI L7→L4, facets S→M). The ZERO NEW TRUTH verdict compares the declared refs to the assembled refs (equality = no fabrication, no loss). A pure function has no OSI section; an API/MCP has the full stack. Check the clean file (no drift, green) or a HAND-EDITED file (the source-hash matches the marker but the bytes differ → HAND_EDITED, red). The same pure function computes the assembly in Go (techspec.Assemble) and here — the judge is a deterministic render + a set comparison + a byte comparison, never a prompt.
techSpec.noDrift: Clean — the file is the exact assembly of the kernel (no drift).
techSpec.zeroTruthOk: OK — the projection assembles EXACTLY the existing technical declarations (no fabrication, no loss).
techSpec.zeroTruthBroken: BROKEN — the assembled refs differ from the declared refs (a new truth would have appeared).
techSpec.driftHandEdited: HAND_EDITED — the body was hand-edited under a valid marker
techSpec.driftMissingMarker: MISSING_MARKER — the file carries no AIDOS source-hash marker
techSpec.driftStaleHash: STALE_HASH — the kernel changed, the file was not re-assembled
techSpec.footer: Read-only projection of back/runtime/generators/techspec — both sheets are assembled (never hand-edited) and write no truth; freezing a projection goes idea → mirror → /goal → human approval.

changeset.title: ChangeSet
changeset.subtitle: KRD §44 · §98
changeset.intro: A ChangeSet is the atomic, reversible transactional envelope that moves the kernel from one stable phase to the next, wrapping spec (Kernel) and mirror (Mirror) together in one body so they can never drift. Its only statuses are DRAFT | APPLIED | REVERTED — there is no FAILED. An APPLIED ChangeSet is immutable; a revert is a new inverse ChangeSet appended to the log (append-only — a revert creates information, it never destroys the source).
changeset.tutorialBody: The envelope card shows the « add order discount » ChangeSet with its spec_delta and mirror_delta side by side — one atomic body, so the spec and its mirror can never drift apart. The lifecycle table runs the state machine: open yields a DRAFT; applying a complete envelope yields APPLIED with a timestamp; applying a spec-without-mirror envelope is blocked (INCOMPLETE_CHANGESET); editing an APPLIED envelope is blocked (APPLIED_IS_IMMUTABLE). The lineage shows that a revert appends a new inverse ChangeSet — the source stays present, stamped REVERTED, never deleted.
changeset.envelopeIntro: One ChangeSet holds both planes: the Kernel spec_delta and the Mirror mirror_delta are stored together, so a spec can never be committed without its mirror.
changeset.atomicNote: Atomic pair — spec and mirror travel together and cannot drift.
changeset.lineageIntro: Reverting an APPLIED envelope appends a new inverse ChangeSet. The source is never destroyed: it stays present, stamped REVERTED, linked from its inverse by reverts.
changeset.stillPresentNote: Still present — stamped REVERTED, never deleted.
changeset.exampleBody: The « add order discount » envelope bundles a spec_delta (add Order.discount) with its mirror_delta (the Order.discount fixture). Applying it is APPLIED with applied_at. Dropping the mirror_delta makes it incomplete — a monster — and the commit-gate blocks it with INCOMPLETE_CHANGESET (how_to_fix: add_mirror_for_spec_delta). Editing it once APPLIED is blocked with APPLIED_IS_IMMUTABLE. Reverting it appends a new DRAFT inverse (cs-B, reverts cs-A) whose later apply stamps cs-A REVERTED — without ever destroying it.
changeset.footer: Read-only projection of back/archive/changeset — a real apply/revert goes through the changeset MCP / the commit-gate (propose → ChangeSet → approval, the wall); an APPLIED envelope is immutable and a revert is append-only.

semanticDiff.title: SemanticDiff
semanticDiff.subtitle: KRD §44.1
semanticDiff.intro: A SemanticDiff reads the real NATURE of a kernel change between two versions (old@hash → new@hash) — KRD §44.1 — instead of a textual line diff, and names it with one member of the closed set this step lands: add · refine · override · rescope · reweight · deprecate. The screen says it in human language ("you are revoking the checkout button's enabled_when promise"), never as a YAML patch.
semanticDiff.tutorialBody: Pick one of the three canonical pairs then run the classification: the screen runs the same pure `classify` that `aidos diff` emits and shows the change_type, the human-language reading, and the referenced blast_radius / requires_authority / red_wave (S15/S16/S17, never recomputed here). A scope change is a rescope, not an override; an incompatible enabled_when is an override (a revoked promise); cosmetic → load-bearing is a reweight. The classification is rendered, never re-implemented in the front-end.
semanticDiff.exampleBody: checkout-button: enabled_when "$.form.valid && !$.submitting" → "$.form.valid" classifies as OVERRIDE. refund-policy: scope EU → EU+US (body identical) classifies as RESCOPE, not override. help-link: composes weight cosmetic → load-bearing classifies as REWEIGHT.
semanticDiff.awaiting: Pick a pair above and run the classification to read the nature of the change.
semanticDiff.footer: aidos diff writes no truth — it reports the nature of a proposed change so a human can decide; applying the change goes through a ChangeSet (the wall).
semanticDiff.sentenceOverride: you are revoking the checkout button's enabled_when promise (the condition loosens) — this is an override, not a mere adjustment; required authority: UX + Product.
semanticDiff.sentenceRescope: you are widening refund-policy's scope from EU to EU+US, the rule body unchanged — this is a rescope, not an override; required authority: Product + Legal.
semanticDiff.sentenceReweight: you are re-qualifying help-link's weight from cosmetic to load-bearing — this is a reweight, a re-qualification of importance, not a change to the rule.

phaseStable.title: Stable phase
phaseStable.subtitle: Coherent DAG cut
phaseStable.intro: A stable phase is a COHERENT CUT in the version DAG (KRD §43): one version per constraint such that EVERY link resolves (S17 green, neither stale nor absent) AND EVERY sensor is green, at once — the kernel's lockfile. "Is this a stable phase?" = "all links resolved + all green?". The empty cut is vacuously STABLE (the base case). ANY single red mirror — a red sensor OR a stale/absent link — makes it UNSTABLE and is named in the reasons.
phaseStable.tutorialBody: Pick a cut from the list, then read the computed verdict. The badge at the top says STABLE or UNSTABLE. The cut shows the constraint→version selection, each link coloured by its resolved status (green = resolves, red = stale/absent) and each sensor green/red. When the cut is unstable, the reasons list names every offending link/sensor. The same pure function computes this verdict in Go (phases.IsStable), in the CLI (aidos stable) and here — one source, no drift. "Stable" is COMPUTED, never declared.
phaseStable.noConstraints: No constraints — the empty cut (the base case).
phaseStable.cutEmpty: Empty cut — vacuously STABLE (the base case, §43)
phaseStable.cutGreen: Green cut — every link resolves, every sensor green (STABLE)
phaseStable.exampleBody: The empty cut is vacuously STABLE: no link pends, nothing is red (the base criterion). A cut where every link resolves and every sensor is green is a STABLE phase. A single red mirror — the createOrder.fixture sensor red — makes the cut UNSTABLE and names it in the reasons (the done criterion). A stale link (checkout-submit pinned to createOrder@v2 off-head) makes the cut pend: UNSTABLE.
phaseStable.footer: Read-only projection of back/archive/phases — the verdict is computed (never declared) and writes no truth; recording the dag.stable_phase node goes via the aidos role inside a ChangeSet.

versionDag.title: Version DAG
versionDag.subtitle: S24 · KRD §120–§125
versionDag.intro: The version space is a DAG, not a line: stable phases are nodes, ChangeSets are edges. Three §121 moves — branch, checkout an ancestor (a backward move), rebranch — grow the DAG append-only with a mutable head. Nothing is ever destroyed: an abandoned line stays as a stepping stone.
versionDag.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive the screen
versionDag.tutorialBody: The graph is stratified by the waterline (§124): human truth above, evolutionary variants below. The current head(s) are highlighted in blue; a node off the path to a head is dimmed — that is the abandoned line, present but off-head (append-only made visible). Click “Branch” to open a line off v1, “Checkout ancestor” to move the head back to v1 (v2 and w1 stay), “Rebranch” to open a new line v2a off v1.
versionDag.eventBranched: Branched — a new line opened (the head moved, nothing deleted)
versionDag.eventHeadMoved: HeadMoved — back to an ancestor (a head-flag move; every later node stays)
versionDag.eventRebranched: Rebranched — a new line off the ancestor (the abandoned line stays)
versionDag.exampleBody: The canonical DAG: a human-truth trunk v0 → v1 → v2 (above) and an evolutionary variant w1 off v1 (below). Branching off v1 opens a parallel head, both lines live (§125). Checking out v1 moves the head back — v2 and w1 remain (append-only). Rebranching off v1 opens a new line v2a, reachable from v0, while the abandoned line v2 stays in the DAG (THE done case).
versionDag.footer: Read-only projection of back/archive/dag — the three §121 moves are pure functions; recording dag.node/dag.edge goes via the aidos writer role through the dag MCP (the wall). The DAG is append-only: an abandoned line is never destroyed.

semanticMerge.title: Semantic merge
semanticMerge.subtitle: S25 · KRD §122/§130
semanticMerge.intro: Merging two truth branches of the version DAG is a SEMANTIC operation, not a textual one. The MIRROR decides the conflict — red on the merged cut (the recursive aggregate §109) — never a line-level three-way diff. A merge git would call "clean" (disjoint deltas, a fast-forward) is BLOCKED when its merged cut reddens a mirror.
semanticMerge.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive the screen
semanticMerge.tutorialBody: Pick a base + left/right triple and run the merge. The verdict renders as a MIRROR DECISION, not a diff: a status badge (clean / conflict), and on conflict the conflicting-mirrors list, a plain sentence, the merged cut (content address) and the required authority. Text-cleanliness NEVER overrides a red mirror — that is THE done criterion.
semanticMerge.conflictingLabel: Conflicting mirrors (red on the merged cut, §122)
semanticMerge.awaiting: Pick a triple and run the merge to see the mirror's verdict.
semanticMerge.overrideAuthority: human (above the waterline) — ChangeSet + ADR + provenance
semanticMerge.sentenceClean: The merged cut's aggregate is GREEN: every link resolves and every mirror (own + composed) is green at once. The merge may proceed — a candidate stable phase (S23), recorded via the ChangeSet path (S20).
semanticMerge.sentenceConflict: git would merge these cleanly, but the merged cut reddens a mirror — this is a CONFLICT (KRD §122). The merge is BLOCKED; resolving it is an override decision (human), never an auto-merge.
semanticMerge.sentenceUnresolvable: Unresolvable merge: no common ancestor (both branches must descend from base, KRD §120). It refuses to guess "clean" — this is an OpenQuestion, never an auto-merge of the unknown.
semanticMerge.exampleBody: Three canonical triples. refund: left pins refund@v2-EU, right refund@v2-US — DISJOINT deltas (git would auto-merge), but the merged cut reddens the refund invariant ⇒ CONFLICT, BLOCKED (THE done criterion: clean text, red mirror). cart: two disjoint-line changes (pay-button / amount-field) break the SAME emergent invariant cart.own_mirror ⇒ CONFLICT (red git never sees). view: a free-space promo banner and help link ⇒ CLEAN (a candidate stable phase).
semanticMerge.footer: Read-only projection of back/archive/merge/MergeSemantic — the decision is a pure function (reusing the coherent-cut oracle phases.IsStable, S23, without forking the aggregate S18 / propagation S19 / red wave S22). No truth write: a clean merge is recorded via the ChangeSet path (S20) under the aidos role (the wall), never from this screen.

archiveCuration.title: Archive curation + QD niches
archiveCuration.subtitle: S26 · KRD §44.4 + §62
archiveCuration.intro: The curation policy keeps the version DAG a LIVING MEMORY rather than an infinite dump by classifying each node keep / compress / tombstone. Critical history is NEVER destroyed: a tombstone MARKS the node (append-only), a compress SUMMARIZES it — neither deletes. The quality-diversity niches (MAP-Elites) keep ONE élite per behavioral niche — a variant enters a niche ONLY IF it has a GREEN mirror (the Judge is the deterministic mirror, never the score).
archiveCuration.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive the screen
archiveCuration.tutorialBody: The curation ledger classifies each DAG node: KEEP (green), COMPRESS (amber), TOMBSTONE (grey) — with its reason, and the note that tombstoned/compressed nodes are STILL PRESENT (append-only). The MAP-Elites grid shows one cell per niche: its single élite and its anchored fitness, or an EMPTY cell when the niche's only candidates have red mirrors ("no promotion without a green mirror" made visible). An unsafe branch is TOMBSTONE (still listed); a green-mirror variant fills its cell.
archiveCuration.stillPresentNote: A tombstone MARKS the node, a compress SUMMARIZES it — the node stays present (append-only); nothing is destroyed (KRD §44.4 / §12).
archiveCuration.emptyCellNote: No promotion: this niche's only candidates have a red mirror (the Judge is the mirror, never the score).
archiveCuration.exampleBody: Ledger: var-7 (unsafe) ⇒ TOMBSTONE, still listed (THE done criterion); phase-3 (stable_phase) and var-2 (pareto_elite) ⇒ KEEP; var-9 (failed > 30d) ⇒ COMPRESS, still present. Grid: niche createOrder/discount is filled by the higher-anchored-fitness champion (var-C, green); niche cancelOrder/refund stays EMPTY — its only candidate (var-B, fitness 0.99) has a RED mirror, so no promotion; niche applyTax/eu keeps var-D (green).
archiveCuration.footer: Read-only projection of back/archive/curation/Curate + back/archive/qd/Elites — pure functions (the bands are DECLARED, not learned; fitness is consumed, never invented; the content hash reuses S01/S02). No truth write: a decision / an élite is recorded via the ChangeSet path (S20) under the aidos role (the wall; the agent is SELECT-only on dag.curation_decision / dag.niche_elite), never from this screen.

exploration.title: Exploration
exploration.subtitle: /grill → /spike → /harvest (ratchet OFF, T0)
exploration.intro: The three exploration gestures over an Idea's lifecycle (KRD §75/§84/§118). /grill challenges the intention ABOVE the wall and routes it on a closed verdict: sharp → grilled (skips the spike); fuzzy → spiking (the floue branch, a ratchet-OFF, T0, throwaway zone); bad → rejected (traced). /spike confines its writes to /spike. /harvest extracts the discovered intention and PROPOSES a DRAFT Truth — a kernel-delta candidate with NO frozen version and NO mirror. The freeze is a separate later /goal.
exploration.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive this screen
exploration.tutorialBody: The status track shows the journey draft → grilled → spiking → harvested (rejected is a traced off-ramp). Run /grill with a verdict: sharp routes to grilled, fuzzy to spiking (ratchet-OFF / T0 badge), bad to rejected. Run the spike writes: the /spike write is allowed, the /kernel write is blocked in RED with SPIKE_WRITE_ESCAPES_ZONE and its fix path. Run /harvest: a DRAFT-Truth card appears, explicitly marked with NO frozen version and NO mirror — promotion needs a /goal.
exploration.exampleBody: The fuzzy intention “something about smarter retries, not sure how” is grilled FUZZY → spiking (ratchet OFF, T0). The spike probes under /spike (allowed); an attempt to write /kernel/retry.policy is blocked by SPIKE_WRITE_ESCAPES_ZONE. Harvest extracts the durable lesson — “retry with capped exponential backoff” — into a DRAFT Truth with NO frozen version and NO mirror, whose provenance points back to the idea. Promoting that DRAFT Truth into a frozen truth is a separate later /goal (which writes the mirror = the freeze).
exploration.footer: KRD §75/§84/§118/§132 · /grill routes, /spike is throwaway and confined, /harvest PROPOSES a DRAFT Truth · the freeze (writing the mirror = /goal) is a separate later gesture · the wall holds (no kernel/mirror write from this screen).
exploration.grillHeading: /grill — challenge the intention and route it
exploration.draftTruthCaveat: DRAFT — no frozen version, no mirror; promotion to truth needs a /goal (which writes the mirror = the freeze).

grillingLoop.title: Grilling loop
grillingLoop.subtitle: executes the /grill verdict
grillingLoop.intro: Grill YOUR intention in product: write the intention and up to five scenarios, NAME the verdict (sharp | fuzzy | bad), and AIDOS routes it DETERMINISTICALLY — sharp → grilled (skips spike), fuzzy → spiking (the fuzzy branch), bad → rejected (traced with its reason). The verdict + provenance are recorded. The routing is AUTHORITATIVE; the LLM is the barricaded exception for the dialogue only, and any verdict it suggests is re-checked against the closed schema before it can route anything.
grillingLoop.tutorialBody: Write your intention, optionally add up to five scenarios (one per line), pick the kind it would become, then NAME the verdict. For "bad", trace a reason. Grill: the idea is routed and appears in the inbox with its lane (grilled / spiking / rejected). A sixth scenario is refused (the ≤ 5 bound is authoritative); an off-schema verdict is refused (the LLM cannot invent a fourth verdict). Promotion to a kernel truth is /goal — never a write from this screen (the wall, CLAUDE.md §2).
grillingLoop.intentPlaceholder: e.g. I want a promo code for regulars
grillingLoop.scenariosPlaceholder: Given a regular When they checkout Then a 10% discount applies
grillingLoop.scenariosHint: At most five scenarios — one per line. A sixth is refused, never silently truncated.
grillingLoop.reasonPlaceholder: e.g. duplicate of an existing policy
grillingLoop.inboxEmpty: No routed idea for this project — grill your first intention.

messages.badVerdict: Off-schema verdict — pick sharp, fuzzy or bad.
messages.tooManyScenarios: At most five scenarios (the ≤ 5 bound is authoritative).
messages.rejectNeedsReason: A bad idea is rejected TRACED — give the reason.
messages.noProject: No active project — pick a project first (the inbox is per-project).
messages.dbUnreachable: Postgres unreachable — the routed idea could not be persisted.

grillingLoop.footer: KRD §75/§118/§132 · /grill routes on a closed verdict (sharp/fuzzy/bad) · DETERMINISTIC, authoritative routing · LLM = barricaded exception for the dialogue, re-checked against the schema · the wall holds (the ideas schema is staging, never the kernel; promotion is /goal).

buildLoop.eyebrow: Workbench/Build · build loop (the executing agent) + deterministic circuit breaker (S83)
buildLoop.title: Build loop
buildLoop.subtitle: S83 · app-builder EPIC 8
buildLoop.intro: The executing agent takes a red set → compiles a ContextPack (S33 algorithm) → calls the LLM → writes code into the sandbox (S82) → runs the affected mirrors → iterates red→green → records the AgentRun (S52). The loop terminates GREEN only when the non-gameable Stop passes; a build that SPENDS WITHOUT ADVANCING stops honestly (BUILD_LOOP_NO_PROGRESS), wired to the HarnessCostBudget (S51). Termination is a PURE FUNCTION OF THE HISTORY, never an LLM judgment.
buildLoop.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive this screen
buildLoop.tutorialBody: Fill in the red set (one mirror per line), the currently-GREEN sensors, the iteration history (one line « diff-hash | comma-separated-green-mirrors »), the Stop conditions (mutation/floor/prior-green/monsters) and the declared budget, then « Evaluate termination ». AIDOS COMPUTES the verdict: GREEN (the non-gameable Stop passes), NO_PROGRESS (repeated diff / oscillation / zero newly-green / cap / over-budget), or CONTINUE. The code is the authority; no truth is written (the wall, §2).
buildLoop.redSetHint: The red mirrors that ARE the goal — one per line.
buildLoop.greenSensorsHint: The red-set mirrors currently GREEN — one per line (the rest are red).
buildLoop.historyHint: One line per turn: « diff-hash | mirror1,mirror2 » (the mirrors green after that turn; the list may be empty).
buildLoop.maxIterationsHint: Hard cap on turns (0 = no cap).
buildLoop.stagnationWindowHint: Consecutive zero-progress turns before halting (≥ 1 to arm).
buildLoop.spentLlmTokensHint: Real measure (S52 counting, never an estimate).
buildLoop.monstersHint: Orphan mirrors / mirror-less truths — one per line; any monster blocks.

verdict.continue: CONTINUE — neither green nor blocked, keep iterating

messages.redSetEmpty: The red set is empty: a goal with no red mirror is not a goal (§56).

buildLoop.footer: KRD §57/§8 · green ONLY when the non-gameable Stop passes (red set→green ∧ prior green intact ∧ mutation ≥ floor ∧ no monster) · the breaker is a PURE FUNCTION of the history (same history → same halt) · BUILD_LOOP_NO_PROGRESS wired to the HarnessCostBudget · the LLM never decides termination, the judge is the mirror + the pure detector · the wall holds (no truth write).

selfCert.eyebrow: Workbench/Build · computational self-certification in the loop (S84)
selfCert.title: Self-certification
selfCert.subtitle: S84 · app-builder EPIC 8
selfCert.intro: At every diff the build loop self-certifies over the REAL sensors — types / lint / unit / fixtures / properties / Pact contract / arch-fitness of the emitted tree (dependency-cruiser). Each iteration is gated: it is GREEN only when ALL sensors pass. A diff that breaks an arch boundary or a Pact contract reddens its sensor and BLOCKS the iteration BEFORE green. The judge is the deterministic mirror, never the LLM (CLAUDE.md §8).
selfCert.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive this screen
selfCert.tutorialBody: For each sensor (types/lint/unit/fixture/property/pact/archfit), check whether it PASSES over the candidate diff; uncheck it to redden it and fill in the detail (the arch boundary / Pact contract / type error that broke), then “Certify the diff”. AIDOS COMPUTES the gated battery: GREEN when all pass, else BUILD_LOOP_SENSOR_RED with the list of red sensors. The code is authoritative; no truth is written (the wall, §2).
selfCert.consoleHint: A missing or red sensor ⇒ not green (anti-passthrough). The full seven-sensor battery gates each iteration.
selfCert.sensorDetailPlaceholder: detail if red (arch boundary / Pact contract / type error)
selfCert.gateRed: RED — the iteration is blocked before green
selfCert.footer: S84 — computational self-certification. Green is computed (the real sensor battery), never declared. The wall (§2): this gate writes no truth.

buildApprovals.eyebrow: Workbench/Build · human approval of the loop's proposed truths (S85)
buildApprovals.title: Build approvals
buildApprovals.subtitle: S85 · app-builder EPIC 8
buildApprovals.intro: When the build loop's work implies a TRUTH, it NEVER writes it directly: it PROPOSES a ChangeSet (proposed, never admitted). A REAL human holding the scope's authority (S52 + S63) approves it from this screen; only THEN does the truth land. The wall holds: an agent write above the waterline is refused AGENT_WRITE_ABOVE_WATERLINE. The judge is the deterministic authority graph, never the LLM (CLAUDE.md §8).
buildApprovals.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive this screen
buildApprovals.tutorialBody: Describe the truth a green build implied (its kernel target, domain, kind, and the GREEN mirror that proves it), then « Propose the truth »: AIDOS PROPOSES it (proposed). A below-the-line target is refused NOT_A_TRUTH_WRITE, a mirror-less truth MISSING_MIRROR. In the inbox, every pending proposal carries its mirror; « Approve » under a human identity holding the scope authority (an owner) ADMITS it; a viewer is refused INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY and the proposal stays proposed. The code is authoritative; the screen writes no truth (the wall, §2).
buildApprovals.proposeHint: The loop PROPOSES — it never writes the truth. The proposal is born `proposed` and carries its mirror; a human admits it below.
buildApprovals.proposedOk: Truth proposed — status: {status} (never admitted from the loop).
buildApprovals.inboxHint: Pending proposals, each with its mirror (no headless approval: you approve what is proven). An admitted proposal has landed and leaves the inbox.
buildApprovals.inboxEmpty: No pending proposal. Propose a truth above.
buildApprovals.admittedMsg: ADMITTED — a human holding the scope authority approved: the truth lands.
buildApprovals.footer: S85 — agent-proposed truth gated at the wall + human approval. The agent PROPOSES, the human ADMITS. The wall (§2): the screen writes no truth; the kernel write stays the `aidos` role via /goal once admitted.

goalPiloting.title: Piloted /goal
goalPiloting.subtitle: open a goal, compute the live red set, non-gameable Stop
goalPiloting.intro: Pilot the /goal from the screen: as a REAL authority-bearing actor (S63), open a goal from a grilled idea. AIDOS PROPOSES a DRAFT ChangeSet (the spec_delta + the mirror_delta, atomically) and computes the REAL red set — the live worklist you see. The Stop is NON-GAMEABLE (§57 ①/§8): closing is refused until all four conditions hold — red set → green ∧ prior green intact ∧ mutation ≥ floor ∧ no monster. "Done" is COMPUTED, never declared.
goalPiloting.tutorialBody: Give your actor identity (never a placeholder nor "agent") and its display name, the source idea, and the red set (the failing mirrors, one per line). Propose the goal: AIDOS returns a DRAFT ChangeSet + the live red set — or a traced refusal (placeholder actor, mirror-less idea, empty red set). Then, in the Stop box, set the four verdicts and check closing: it is refused (GOAL_STILL_RED) until all four hold. The screen PROPOSES a ChangeSet, it NEVER writes the Kernel (the wall, CLAUDE.md §2) — persistence rides the changeset door (S20) + approval (S85).
goalPiloting.proposeHeading: Open a goal (propose a DRAFT ChangeSet)
goalPiloting.redSetLabel: Live red set (the failing mirrors, one per line)
goalPiloting.redSetHint: The red mirrors that ARE the goal (§56: the red set IS the todo-list). An empty set is refused.
goalPiloting.hasMirrorLabel: The idea carries a mirror_delta (otherwise: a wish, refused)
goalPiloting.wallNote: The screen PROPOSES — it never writes the Kernel (the wall).
goalPiloting.closeAccepted: Closing admitted — all four conditions hold.
goalPiloting.closeRefused: Closing refused (GOAL_STILL_RED) — at least one condition fails.

messages.proposeOk: Goal proposed — DRAFT ChangeSet + live red set (awaiting approval, the Kernel is not written).

goalPiloting.footer: KRD §56–§59/§63 ① · the screen PROPOSES a DRAFT ChangeSet, NEVER writes the Kernel · real actor via S63 (never a placeholder) · LIVE red set · NON-GAMEABLE Stop: red set→green ∧ prior green intact ∧ mutation ≥ floor ∧ no monster.

ideas.title: Ideas
ideas.subtitle: draft → grilled → {spiking → harvested} → /goal
ideas.intro: An idea is a CANDIDATE-truth above product but below the freeze: a sketched body — proposes + intent + provenance — with NO version-freeze and NO mirror. That double absence is exactly what makes it an idea and not a truth. "Promote" is not a status: it is the act of writing the idea's mirror, which IS the /goal, which IS the freeze into /kernel.
ideas.tutorialHeading: How to read and drive this screen
ideas.tutorialBody: Each card shows an idea — its proposes (the targeted layer), its intent (the sketched behaviour), its provenance (the human utterance or the incident) and its status — with a "no mirror yet" marker. Cards are grouped into the five lifecycle lanes. Below, run the promotion of the harvested idea two ways: WITHOUT a mirror → a red NO_MIRROR_NO_KERNEL refusal and the idea STAYS harvested (no kernel write); WITH a mirror → the Promoted → /goal → frozen-truth path, with the provenance link pointing back to the idea.
ideas.exampleBody: The idea "regulars get a discount" is captured (draft), grilled, explored (spiking), then harvested. Promoted WITHOUT a mirror it is blocked by NO_MIRROR_NO_KERNEL (fix: write_mirror_run_goal_freeze) and stays harvested. Promoted WITH its red mirror it flows through /goal to a frozen kernel truth whose provenance points back to the idea. A rejected idea ("discount for everyone") stays visible in the rejected lane — traced, never deleted.
ideas.footer: KRD §115/§116/§118/§119 · the only idea → truth path is the mirror and the /goal · the kernel has no other key.
ideas.promoteHeading: Promotion — the only door to the kernel
ideas.staysHarvestedNote: The idea stays harvested — no kernel write.

captureIdea.title: Capture your idea
captureIdea.subtitle: provenance: human
captureIdea.intro: Type YOUR intention in free text: AIDOS content-addresses it (the same hash the engine computes) and writes a REAL idea record — a draft — into the truth-store, scoped to YOUR active project. An idea is a CANDIDATE-truth: a sketched body (proposes + intent + provenance) with NO freeze and NO mirror. The inbox below lists ONLY your project's ideas — the per-project inbox that replaces the /ideas fixture.
captureIdea.tutorialBody: Write your intention, pick the kind it would become if promoted, optionally say who is asking, then Capture. The idea appears immediately in your active project's inbox, with its provenance and the "no mirror yet" marker. Promotion to a kernel truth is /goal — never a write from this screen (the wall, CLAUDE.md §2).
captureIdea.intentPlaceholder: e.g. I want a cart discount for regulars
captureIdea.inboxEmpty: No idea captured for this project yet — your first intention will appear here.

messages.captureNoProject: No active project — pick a project first (the inbox is per-project).
messages.dbUnreachable: Postgres unreachable — the idea could not be persisted.

captureIdea.footer: Below the wall: the ideas schema is staging above the line (a candidate-truth), never the kernel. Promotion to a frozen truth goes through /goal.

goal.title: Goal
goal.subtitle: idea → mirror → /goal · non-gameable stop (§57 ①)
goal.intro: The only legitimate door from an idea to truth (KRD §56–§59, §63 ①, BOOK XX): idea → mirror → /goal. A goal is a DRAFT ChangeSet (S20) carrying the idea's spec_delta + mirror_delta atomically PLUS the RED SET — the failing mirrors that ARE the goal (§56: "the red test IS the goal; the red set IS the todo-list"). The stop is NON-GAMEABLE: a goal closes ONLY when the red set turns green ∧ prior green stays intact ∧ mutation ≥ floor ∧ no monster — never on the agent's say-so. "Done" is computed, never declared.
goal.tutorialHeading: How to read and drive this screen
goal.tutorialBody: Click "Open the goal": from the canonical idea idea-order-discount, the engine opens a DRAFT ChangeSet and derives a non-empty red set (the done criterion, visible on screen) — status OPEN, the stop NOT satisfied while any mirror is red. Click "Check the stop (red)" / "(green)" to watch the stop indicator compute its four conditions: the red set closes only when all four hold. The agent never closes it itself: the aidos role stamps CLOSED via the commit-gate (S20).
goal.exampleBody: The idea idea-order-discount proposes Order.discount with its mirror Order.discount.fixture. /goal opens a DRAFT ChangeSet (atomic spec_delta + mirror_delta) and derives the red set { Order.discount.fixture } via the red wave (S22). While that mirror is red, the stop reads NOT satisfied. When it turns green and prior green is intact (mutation ≥ 0.8, no monster), all four conditions hold and the stop reads satisfied — the goal becomes closeable, but the aidos role stamps it, never the agent.
goal.footer: Goal engine — internal loop ① only (not the /evolve loop ②, not the reality loop ③). The red-set derivation is consumed from S22, the ChangeSet envelope + commit-gate from S20, the SemanticDiff from S21; none is redefined here. The engine never reads the agent's confidence.
goal.stopNotSatisfied: NOT satisfied — the goal stays OPEN
goal.closeNote: "Done" is computed, never declared: the engine never reads the agent's confidence. The close runs through the Stop:goal-check hook and the aidos role (S20 commit-gate), never the agent.

memoryFirewall.title: MemoryFirewall
memoryFirewall.subtitle: memory proposes, the kernel declares
memoryFirewall.intro: The MemoryFirewall (KRD §119.1) is the gate of the /brain store: no MemoryItem reaches the kernel except through the mandatory one-way flow Memory → ContextPack → Idea → Mirror → Goal → Kernel. A MemoryItem is context fuel, NEVER a truth: no version-freeze, no mirror. The direct Memory → Kernel edge is ALWAYS blocked — regardless of its confidence or taint. “Memory proposes; the kernel declares the true.”
memoryFirewall.tutorialHeading: How to read & drive this screen
memoryFirewall.tutorialBody: Capture the memory (a MemoryItem — fuel, not truth). Propose it into a ContextPack: the taint travels with the entry (allowed). Attempt to-kernel: it is ALWAYS blocked (MEMORY_CANNOT_DECLARE_TRUTH, no kernel write). Take via-idea: the memory becomes a draft idea (S27) whose provenance points back to the memory — and which STILL has no mirror, so it is still short of the kernel.
memoryFirewall.exampleBody: “regulars always get 20% off” — a user_claim that is stale, confidence 0.4. Proposable into a ContextPack with its taint; blocked at the direct edge to the kernel; routable into a draft idea that must still acquire its mirror via /goal.
memoryFirewall.footer: Read-only against truth. The /brain store is below the waterline (the agent reads and appends memory); the freeze into /kernel is written by the aidos role via /goal, never by memory or the agent.
memoryFirewall.notTruthMarker: not truth — no mirror, no freeze
memoryFirewall.taintTravels: The taint travels with the entry — never silently dropped.
memoryFirewall.blockedHeading: Blocked — memory cannot declare the truth
memoryFirewall.viaIdeaHeading: The only legal door — via an idea (S27)

memoryBackends.title: Memory backends
memoryBackends.subtitle: write + similarity recall (pgvector)
memoryBackends.intro: The /brain store's memory adapter (KRD §136): write a MemoryItem and recall it by similarity over pgvector embeddings, across the four INDEXABLE memories — episodic / semantic / procedural / structural. Working memory (the live context window) and evolutionary memory (the S24 version DAG) are NOT here. Two injectable backends behind one interface (deterministic mock ↔ real pgvector): the toggle makes the injection seam observable. Context fuel, NEVER truth.
memoryBackends.tutorialHeading: How to read and drive this screen
memoryBackends.tutorialBody: Pick a backend (mock ↔ real): the toggle re-runs recall through the other Store — the same top hit returns, so the backends are interchangeable. Filter by kind (the four indexable memories). Enter a recall query: hits appear ordered by score descending, nearest first. Each hit shows score / kind / branch / taint / provenance — memory is fuel WITH provenance, never silent truth.
memoryBackends.exampleBody: Query 'shopping cart basket' over the four kinds: the semantic 'shopping cart' term ranks first (nearest by similarity). The kind=semantic + branch=main filter excludes the branch-x semantic row; flipping mock ↔ real returns the same top hit (both backends injectable behind the same interface).
memoryBackends.footer: Read-only against truth. The /brain store is below the waterline (the agent reads and appends memory); nothing here reaches the kernel without a mirror — the MemoryFirewall flow (§119.1) is a separate concern.
memoryBackends.banner: Context fuel, never truth — nothing here reaches the kernel without a mirror.
memoryBackends.seamNote: Flipping the backend re-runs recall through the other Store: the same top hit returns (the backends are interchangeable behind one interface).

decisionReuse.title: ContextGraphDecision
decisionReuse.subtitle: reuse, permitted or blocked
